newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Daimler sees profits jumping.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Daimler sees profits jumping.

text.p: Germany's Daimler-Benz AG, reporting a 12 percent rise in first quarter sales, predicted on Wednesday profits could grow strongly by the turn of the century as its restructuring plan takes hold.

Daimler chief executive Juergen Schrempp, who has orchestrated a major reorganisation at Daimler, told the group's annual news conference that Daimler's goal of a 12 percent return on capital could be reached within two years.
"Our productivity and efficiency initiatives are showing their initial success," Schrempp said. "In 1997 we will not let ourselves be measured by words, but by deeds."
Schrempp's upbeat forecast suggests a hefty increase in Daimler's 1996 operating profit level of 2.42 billion marks ($1.4 billion) could be in store for the coming years.
Daimler chief financial officer Manfred Gentz said Daimler's goal of a 12 percent return on capital employed compared with the current level of five to six percent could be met in two years.

Asked later if the two statements taken together meant that operating profit was set to double, Daimler officials declined to give a specific forecast but said operating profit could be set for a substantial rise -- barring a blow to its finances.
Daimler, Germany's largest industrial group, was ready to back up its forecasts after announcing on Wednesday that first quarter sales rose 12 percent to 25.9 billion marks.

Daimler shares were among the heaviest-traded in dealings on Wednesday, rising in IBIS electronic trade to an all-time high of 142.15 marks before falling 1.30 marks to 138 marks after Daimler set plans for a 1.1 billion mark offering.

Daimler credited its optimistic outlook to expectations of sales growth for its Mercedes-Benz cars and trucks unit and a return to profitability in 1997 for its aircraft and space unit, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA).
Breaking down its 1996 profits for the first time, the Mercedes vehicle division, which gave 2.7 billion marks to the group's 1996 operating profit, was again the top quarterly revenue source.

Despite expectations for limited growth in the vehicle markets in the coming months, Daimler said its own business would "develop significantly more favourably than the industry on the whole in 1997".

Daimler also noted the recovery at its Dasa aerospace unit, which narrowed its consolidated operating loss to 196 million marks in 1996 compared with 7.2 billion marks in 1995, and prediction sales would "grow markedly" during the year.
"We recognise that Daimler-Benz has only completed the first step on the road toward becoming one of the world's leading corporations," Schrempp said.

The rosy outlook comes as a vindication for Schrempp who been harshly criticized by unions for his determination to cut costs and who pushed through an overhaul of Daimler in January, over the objections of the respected Mercedes-Benz chief Helmut Werner.
Indeed, the Daimler board last year was forced to admit it had made mistakes in its business strategies, announcing a 5.7 billion mark net loss for 1995 - the largest in German history.

Carrying the tax losses forward from 1995 and the restructuring, which were mostly due to write-downs of its AEG engineering and consumer products company and Dutch aircraft unit Fokker NV, helped give 1996's profits a boost.
Gentz said net income got a 700 million mark boost from deferred tax loss credits stemming from last year's losses.

On a day of mostly upbeat news for Daimler, stock traders were disappointed at Daimler's plan to increase capital when the company announced it would raise approximately 1.1 billion marks in mandatory convertible notes.
Daimler said that the instrument will be converted into Daimler shares in 2002 at the latest, when the issue reaches maturity.
($ = 1.726 German Marks)
